title: Going Concern and Bankruptcy Prediction under Extreme Class Imbalance: Cost-Sensitive Learning, Resampling, and Focal Loss with Explainable Financial-Ratio Portraits
authors: Chen, Y.; Zhang, Y.; Sherman, M.
tldr: Evaluates cost-sensitive learning, resampling, and focal loss for bankruptcy prediction under extreme imbalance on the Polish Companies dataset, finding tree ensembles with missing indicators achieve best AUPRC.
problem_and_motivation: Going-concern prediction involves extreme class imbalance (fewer than 5% firms fail) where misclassifying a distressed firm is far costlier than false alarms. Standard classifiers suffer from bias toward the majority class and evaluation metrics like accuracy are misleading.
approach: Uses the Polish Companies Bankruptcy benchmark (64 financial ratios, 43,405 firm-year records, five forecasting horizons) from UCI.
Compares three imbalance-aware strategy families: cost-sensitive learning via class-weighted objectives, resampling (ROS, RUS, SMOTE), and focal loss.
Base learners are logistic regression and random forest with 200 trees.
Evaluates using AUPRC and Recall@Top-k with k values from 0.5% to 20%.
Augments features with binary missing-value indicators to exploit missingness as a predictive signal.
findings: num: Cost-sensitive random forest with missing indicators achieved AUPRC of 0.640 (1stYear), 0.480, 0.459, 0.567, and 0.601 for five horizons.
num: Augmenting with missing-value indicators increased AUPRC from 0.480 to 0.640 in the 1stYear case.
num: Auditing top 5% of firms ranked by best model recovered 62.96% of bankruptcies vs 12.35% for logistic regression.
Tree ensembles dominated linear models across all five forecasting horizons.
Focal loss did not provide consistent gains over cost-sensitive weighting.
key_figures_tables: Table 3: Financial ratios subset used in explainability analysis.

key_equations.equation: Recall@Top-k = fraction of bankrupt firms in audited top-k subset
key_equations.explanation: Proportion of bankruptcies captured within review budget.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper provides a reproducible empirical comparison of three imbalance-handling strategy families for bankruptcy prediction across five forecasting horizons. It demonstrates that missingness patterns carry predictive signal that can substantially improve AUPRC, and that audit-oriented metrics like Recall@Top-k provide operationally meaningful evaluation. The explainable financial-ratio portrait bridges predictive modeling with actionable accounting evidence.
directly_justifies: Missing-value indicators improved AUPRC from 0.480 to 0.640 in 1stYear case.
Recall@Top-5% recovered 62.96% of bankruptcies vs 12.35% for logistic regression.
Tree ensembles dominated linear models across all five forecasting horizons.
limits: Single dataset (Polish Companies) limits generalizability to other economies.
Focal loss evaluation limited to logistic regression, not tested with tree ensembles.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: Systematic scan across all 14 topic domains was conducted. Topics 6.A (Predictive Modeling) and 8.A (Anomaly Detection) were rated high as the paper addresses bankruptcy prediction under extreme imbalance. Topic 6.B (Forecasting Algorithms) was rated medium as the approach spans multiple time horizons. Topic 8.B (Anomaly Detection Algorithms) was rated medium for its comparison of imbalance-handling techniques. Topics 1.x-5.x, 7.x, 9.x-14.x were rejected as the paper focuses on financial ratio-based bankruptcy prediction, not personal finance system design.

limitations: Single dataset from Polish companies limits cross-economy generalizability.
Focal loss only evaluated on logistic regression, not on tree ensembles.
No investigation of deep learning alternatives beyond tree ensembles.
